claim: Leonid meteors hit at about 43.5 miles per second; they are debris from comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle (33-year orbit), and storms of 1,000+ per hour recur about every 33 years, last in 2002.

beats.caption: 43 miles per second
beats.vo: These meteors hit at 43 miles per second.

beats.caption: Comet dust
beats.vo: They're the Leonids: dust and debris shed by comet Tempel-Tuttle, which circles the Sun once every 33 years.

beats.caption: Earth plows through the trail
beats.vo: Each November, Earth plows through that trail. The grains hit our air at about 43 and a half miles per second, which makes the Leonids some of the fastest meteors we see.

beats.caption: Storm every ~33 years
beats.vo: Every 33 years or so, that can become a storm of over a thousand meteors an hour. The last was in 2002. This year? Fewer than three an hour. Will you still look up on November 16th?

sources.text: NASA Science, Leonids: 43.5 mi (69.7 km) per second; comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, 33-year orbit; storm (1,000+/hour) about every 33 years, last in 2002; 2026 active Nov 6-30, peak Nov 16-17, fewer than 3 per hour under dark skies. https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/leonids/
